annotations.text: LLM-based judges are widely used to evaluate web agent trajectories, but they are vulnerable to manipulation through unfaithful chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We propose view-disagreement escalation, a training-free framework that compares judgments from two counterfactual input views—one with CoT and one without—to detect unreliable predictions. When views disagree, we escalate to strict evidence-anchored evaluation. Our key insight is that CoT manipulation affects CoT-dependent judgments while leaving CoT-agnostic judgments stable, causing disagreement that signals potential manipulation. On AgentReward-Bench, our method achieves 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity (∆-FPR: 4.31% vs 11.71%) while maintaining competitive F1 (72.13% vs 72.93%) and achieving the best recall (77.63%). The 2.15× disagreement enrichment under attack validates our mechanistic hypothesis.
annotations.comment:
The abstract is well-structured but contains two issues that affect claim defensibility.

(Audit) The claim "63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity" compares against View1-only (Δ-FPR 4.31% vs. 11.71%), but View2-only and Strict-always achieve 0.00% Δ-FPR (Table 1). This means the method is not the most robust; it is the most balanced between robustness and accuracy. The abstract should explicitly bound this comparison rather than implying overall best robustness.

(Audit) The statement "achieving the best recall (77.63%)" is accurate per Table 1, but the abstract does not mention that Random Escalation achieves nearly identical F1 (72.41% vs. 72.13%). Omitting this context risks overstating the method's advantage.

(Risk) The abstraction-level claim of "63% relative reduction" without qualification could mislead readers into thinking this is the maximum achievable robustness improvement, when View2-only achieves zero sensitivity at the cost of F1.

(Mentor Revised Version) LLM-based judges are widely used to evaluate web agent trajectories, but they are vulnerable to manipulation through unfaithful chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We propose view-disagreement escalation, a training-free framework that compares judgments from two counterfactual input views—one with CoT and one without—to detect unreliable predictions. When views disagree, we escalate to strict evidence-anchored evaluation. Our key insight is that CoT manipulation affects CoT-dependent judgments while leaving CoT-agnostic judgments stable, causing disagreement that signals potential manipulation. On AgentRewardBench, our method achieves a 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity (Δ-FPR: 4.31% vs. 11.71%) compared to standard CoT-inclusive judging, while maintaining competitive F1 (72.13%) and the best recall (77.63%). The 2.15× disagreement enrichment under attack validates our mechanistic hypothesis.
annotations.summary: Abstract claims "63% relative reduction" but View2-only achieves 0% Δ-FPR; the framing should clarify the method balances robustness with accuracy, not maximizes robustness alone.

annotations.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as judges to evaluate web agent trajectories, providing scalable assessment of whether agents successfully complete tasks (Zheng et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2025). This LLM-as-a-judge paradigm enables automatic evaluation at scale, sup-\` porting both benchmarking and training data selection for agent improvement. However, the reliability of these judges is critical: when judge outputs are used for rejection sampling or reward signals, false positives can inject label noise and enable reward hacking.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) This first introduction paragraph effectively establishes the practical stakes: LLM-as-a-judge is used for trajectory evaluation, and false positives are costly (label noise, reward hacking). The problem alignment with the proposed solution is clear.

(Diagnosis) However, the paragraph does not explicitly state what is missing in prior work. It identifies a risk (judge unreliability) but does not yet explain why existing methods cannot solve it, leaving the reader unclear about the specific research gap.

(Risk) Without a sharper gap statement, the motivation for the method feels like an incremental engineering fix rather than a conceptually driven approach.

(Mentor Revised Version) Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as judges to evaluate web agent trajectories, providing scalable assessment of whether agents successfully complete tasks (Zheng et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2025). This LLM-as-a-judge paradigm enables automatic evaluation at scale, supporting both benchmarking and training data selection for agent improvement. However, the reliability of these judges is critical: when judge outputs are used for rejection sampling or reward signals, false positives can inject label noise and enable reward hacking. Current evaluation approaches do not distinguish between trustworthy and manipulated judgments, leaving the system vulnerable to CoT-based attacks without a principled detection mechanism.
annotations.summary: Intro P1 establishes stakes well but lacks explicit research gap; adding what prior work misses strengthens the method's conceptual positioning.

annotations.text: A key vulnerability emerges from the judge’s reliance on agent-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces. Khalifa et al. (2026) demonstrated that manipulating only the CoT—while keeping actions and observations fixed—can inflate false positive rates by up to 90%. This attack exploits the judge’s tendency to trust persuasive narrative reasoning that is not grounded in observable evidence. Existing mitigations face a fundamental trade-off: removing CoT entirely eliminates the vulnerability but sacrifices useful context for interpreting agent behavior, while always-on strict evaluation increases cost and can reduce recall.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) This paragraph clearly articulates the core vulnerability: CoT manipulation can inflate FPR by up to 90%, and existing mitigations face a trade-off between robustness and accuracy. The citation of Khalifa et al. (2026) is appropriate and well-grounded.

(Diagnosis) The paragraph sets up the problem well, but it does not explicitly connect the trade-off to the proposed solution. The phrase "Existing mitigations face a fundamental trade-off" is accurate, but it could be strengthened by explicitly stating what the paper does differently—namely, that it selectively applies strict evaluation only when needed.

(Risk) Without this explicit link, the transition to the next paragraph feels slightly abrupt, and the reader may not immediately grasp how the proposed method resolves the trade-off.

(Mentor Revised Version) A key vulnerability emerges from the judge's reliance on agent-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces. Khalifa et al. (2026) demonstrated that manipulating only the CoT—while keeping actions and observations fixed—can inflate false positive rates by up to 90%. This attack exploits the judge's tendency to trust persuasive narrative reasoning that is not grounded in observable evidence. Existing mitigations face a fundamental trade-off: removing CoT entirely eliminates the vulnerability but sacrifices useful context for interpreting agent behavior, while always-on strict evaluation increases cost and can reduce recall. To break this trade-off, we need a method that selectively applies strict evaluation only when CoT manipulation is likely, preserving both robustness and accuracy.
annotations.summary: Intro P2 explains the CoT vulnerability and trade-off well, but could explicitly link the trade-off to the proposed selective escalation approach.

annotations.text:
• Empirical validation that view disagreement is enriched under CoT manipulation attacks (2.15× higher disagreement rate on attacked vs. unmodified failures), confirming the mechanistic hypothesis.
• Demonstration that our method achieves 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity (∆- FPR: 4.31% vs 11.71%) while maintaining competitive F1 (72.13% vs 72.93%) and achieving the best recall (77.63%) on AgentRewardBench.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) The three contribution claims are well-specified and map directly to the paper's core innovations: (C1) the framework itself, (C2) mechanistic validation via disagreement enrichment, and (C3) empirical robustness gains.

(Diagnosis) Contribution 3 mixes two types of evidence: a comparative claim ("63% relative reduction") and an absolute claim ("best recall"). While both are empirically supported, the contribution list reads somewhat like a results summary rather than a conceptual contribution statement. Consider reframing to emphasize the methodological contribution (trade-off resolution) over the performance numbers.

(Risk) Over-indexing on metrics in the contribution list can make the paper appear incremental. Reviewers may perceive the core contribution as engineering-level rather than conceptual.

(Mentor Revised Version) Our contributions are:

• A mechanistically-motivated framework that uses counterfactual input views (with/without CoT) to detect unreliable predictions and selectively escalate to strict evidence-anchored judgment, breaking the trade-off between robustness and accuracy.

• Empirical validation that view disagreement is enriched under CoT manipulation attacks (2.15× higher disagreement rate on attacked vs. unmodified failures), confirming that disagreement is a reliable signal for detecting manipulation.

• Demonstration on AgentRewardBench that our method achieves a 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity compared to standard CoT-inclusive judging, while maintaining competitive F1 and achieving the best recall, showing that selective escalation provides a robustness-accuracy balance that neither CoT-only nor CoT-agnostic baselines achieve.
annotations.summary: Contribution bullets mix metrics with conceptual claims; reframe C3 to emphasize the trade-off resolution as the core contribution rather than just performance numbers.

annotations.text: Robustness of LLM Judges. Prior work has identified several vulnerabilities in LLM judges, including position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias (Zheng et al., 2023). More critically, Khalifa et al. (2026) demonstrated that LLM judges are highly susceptible to manipulation through unfaithful CoT reasoning. By rewriting agent reasoning traces while holding actions fixed, they showed that manipulated CoT can inflate false positive rates by up to 90%. This vulnerability is particularly concerning for trajectory evaluation, where judges naturally rely on CoT to understand agent behavior. Evidence-anchored evaluation approaches like RULERS (Hong et al., 2026) attempt to ground judgments in concrete evidence, but the fundamental tension between utilizing informative CoT and avoiding manipulation remains unresolved.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) The Related Work section is well-organized into four thematic paragraphs: LLM-as-a-Judge, Robustness of LLM Judges, Selective Prediction and Escalation, and Web Agent Benchmarks. Each paragraph correctly positions prior work and identifies the gap.

(Diagnosis) The "Robustness of LLM Judges" paragraph correctly cites Khalifa et al. (2026) as the primary prior work on CoT manipulation, but it omits discussion of recent concurrent work on judge consistency and rationalization bias (e.g., ConsJudge by Liu et al., 2025; Faithful or Fabricated by Tapwal et al., 2026). These papers explore similar themes of judge reliability and evidence-anchored prompting, which strengthens the novelty claim if explicitly differentiated.

(Risk) Without citing these related works, reviewers may question whether the paper's approach is truly novel or simply an alternative formulation of judge-consistency methods. The paper should explicitly distinguish its counterfactual view disagreement from ConsJudge's dimension-wise consistency and from Tapwal et al.'s PROOF-BEFORE-PREFERENCE protocol.

(Mentor Revised Version) Robustness of LLM Judges. Prior work has identified several vulnerabilities in LLM judges, including position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias (Zheng et al., 2023). More critically, Khalifa et al. (2026) demonstrated that LLM judges are highly susceptible to manipulation through unfaithful CoT reasoning, showing that manipulated CoT can inflate false positive rates by up to 90%. This vulnerability is particularly concerning for trajectory evaluation, where judges naturally rely on CoT to understand agent behavior. Recent work has explored judge consistency across evaluation dimensions (ConsJudge; Liu et al., 2025) and cue-invariance in judge rationalizations (Tapwal et al., 2026), but these approaches do not address the specific asymmetric threat of CoT manipulation in web agent evaluation. Evidence-anchored evaluation approaches like RULERS (Hong et al., 2026) attempt to ground judgments in concrete evidence, but the fundamental tension between utilizing informative CoT and avoiding manipulation remains unresolved.
annotations.summary: Related Work omits ConsJudge (2025) and Faithful or Fabricated (2026), which explore judge consistency and rationalization bias; this weakens novelty positioning.

annotations.text: A web-agent trajectory τ consists of a task goal g, a sequence of actions $\{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { T } \}$ , observations of page states, and optionally an agent-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning trace c. The trajectory evaluation task is to predict whether the agent successfully completed the goal: $\hat { y } \in$ {success, failure}.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) The Method section opening is concise and clearly states the two-stage nature of the framework. The problem setup (Section 3.1) provides a clean formal definition of a trajectory τ and the evaluation task.

(Diagnosis) The notation is well-defined, but one potential ambiguity exists: "evidence" is not formally defined in the trajectory tuple, though it appears implicitly in Section 3.2 (View1 and View2 definitions). The trajectory definition mentions "observations of page states," but later formulations use "evidence" as a distinct component. Clarifying this mapping improves reproducibility.

(Risk) Ambiguity between "observations" and "evidence" could confuse implementers trying to reproduce the setup.

(Mentor Revised Version) A web-agent trajectory τ consists of a task goal g, a sequence of actions $\{a_1, \ldots, a_T\}$, observations of page states (denoted as evidence), and optionally an agent-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning trace c. The trajectory evaluation task is to predict whether the agent successfully completed the goal: $\hat{y} \in \{\text{success}, \text{failure}\}$. Here, "evidence" refers to the sequence of observable page states and action outcomes that ground the evaluation, excluding the agent's internal reasoning trace.
annotations.summary: Section 3.1 trajectory tuple uses "observations" but later sections use "evidence"; clarify the mapping for reproducibility.

annotations.text:
Our key insight is that CoT manipulation exploits the judge’s reliance on narrative reasoning traces. A judge that does not see the CoT cannot be manipulated by it. This asymmetry motivates comparing judgments from two counterfactual input views of the same trajectory:
View1 (with CoT). The judge receives the complete trajectory including the agent’s reasoning trace: View $\mathbf l ( \tau ) = ( g , \{ a _ { t } \}$ }, evidence, c). This view provides rich context for understanding agent intent but is susceptible to persuasive but unfaithful reasoning.
View2 (without CoT). The judge receives only observable evidence: $\begin{array} { r l } { \mathrm { V i e w } 2 ( \tau ) } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $\left( g , \{ a _ { t } \} \right)$ , evidence). This view is agnostic to CoT manipulation since the reasoning trace is excluded, but may miss useful context for interpreting ambiguous actions.
The mechanistic hypothesis is that when CoT is manipulated (e.g., fabricating progress claims), View1 predictions will shift toward false positives while View2 predictions remain stable. Therefore, disagreement between views— $- y _ { 1 } ~ \ne ~ y _ { 2 }$ —should be enriched on trajectories where the judge is unreliable due to CoT manipulation.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) The mechanistic hypothesis is the conceptual core of the paper: CoT manipulation shifts View1 but leaves View2 stable, causing disagreement. This is an elegant and testable claim.

(Diagnosis) However, the assumption that View2 "remains stable" under CoT manipulation is not fully justified. In practice, removing CoT can change the judge's reasoning even for unmanipulated trajectories, because CoT may contain legitimate context that helps the judge interpret ambiguous actions. The paper should explicitly acknowledge that View2 is not perfectly stable—it is only stable with respect to CoT manipulation effects. This distinction matters for interpreting the disagreement signal.

(Risk) If View2 predictions are inherently unstable due to CoT removal (not manipulation), then disagreement could be inflated on unmanipulated trajectories, reducing the specificity of the escalation trigger. The experimental results show 7.6% disagreement on unmodified failures, which partially validates concern.

(Mentor Revised Version) Our key insight is that CoT manipulation exploits the judge's reliance on narrative reasoning traces. A judge that does not see the CoT cannot be manipulated by it. This asymmetry motivates comparing judgments from two counterfactual input views of the same trajectory:

View1 (with CoT). The judge receives the complete trajectory including the agent's reasoning trace: View1(τ) = (g, {at}, evidence, c). This view provides rich context for understanding agent intent but is susceptible to persuasive but unfaithful reasoning.

View2 (without CoT). The judge receives only observable evidence: View2(τ) = (g, {at}, evidence). This view is agnostic to CoT manipulation since the reasoning trace is excluded, though it may miss useful context for interpreting ambiguous actions.

The mechanistic hypothesis is that when CoT is manipulated (e.g., fabricating progress claims), View1 predictions will shift toward false positives while View2 predictions remain relatively stable. Therefore, disagreement between views (y1 ≠ y2) should be enriched on trajectories where the judge is unreliable due to CoT manipulation. We note that View2 is not perfectly stable—removing CoT can change judgments even for unmanipulated trajectories—but the key assumption is that manipulation-induced shifts are asymmetric, disproportionately affecting View1.
annotations.summary: The mechanistic hypothesis assumes View2 stability under manipulation, but CoT removal inherently changes judge behavior; clarify this assumption to strengthen conceptual rigor.

annotations.text:
3.3 DISAGREEMENT DETECTION AND ESCALATION
We implement a two-stage evaluation pipeline:
Stage 1: Dual-View Judging. Run a base judge prompt $P _ { \mathrm { b a s e } }$ on both views to obtain predictions $y _ { 1 }$ and $y _ { 2 }$ . We use deterministic decoding (temperature=0) to ensure disagreement reflects view differences rather than sampling noise.
Stage 2: Selective Escalation. If $y _ { 1 } = y _ { 2 }$ , output the agreed prediction. If $y _ { 1 } \neq y _ { 2 }$ , escalate to a strict evidence-anchored rubric prompt $P _ { \mathrm { s t r i c t } }$ that:
• Excludes all agent-generated reasoning traces
• Requires explicit citation of evidence from actions and final-state artifacts
• Uses a structured checklist of task requirements
• Outputs a machine-parseable judgment with evidence justification
The final prediction is:
$$
\hat {y} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} y _ {1} & \text {if} y _ {1} = y _ {2} \\ y _ {\text {strict}} & \text {if} y _ {1} \neq y _ {2} \end{array} \right.\tag{1}
$$
This design applies the more expensive strict evaluation only when the disagreement signal indicates potential unreliability, achieving a better precision-recall-cost trade-off than always-on strict evaluation.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) Section 3.3 clearly defines the two-stage pipeline: dual-view judging followed by selective escalation to strict evidence-anchored rubric. The equation (1) formalizes the final prediction logic concisely.

(Diagnosis) The strict rubric prompt $P_{\text{strict}}$ is described by its characteristics (excludes CoT, requires evidence citation, uses checklist, outputs machine-parseable judgment), but the actual rubric design is not specified. How are the "structured checklist of task requirements" constructed? Are they derived from the task goal g, from benchmark definitions, or from a template? This detail is critical for reproducibility.

(Risk) Without specifying how the strict rubric is constructed, the method cannot be faithfully reproduced. Reviewers will need to know whether the rubric is task-specific, manually crafted, or automatically generated.

(Mentor Revised Version) Stage 2: Selective Escalation. If $y_1 = y_2$, output the agreed prediction. If $y_1 \neq y_2$, escalate to a strict evidence-anchored rubric prompt $P_{\text{strict}}$ that:

• Excludes all agent-generated reasoning traces
• Requires explicit citation of evidence from actions and final-state artifacts
• Uses a structured checklist of task requirements (derived from the benchmark task definitions, including success criteria and required outcomes)
• Outputs a machine-parseable judgment with evidence justification

The strict rubric is constructed from the task's ground-truth evaluation criteria as provided in AgentRewardBench. For tasks without explicit success criteria, we use a generic rubric requiring the agent to achieve the stated goal without side effects. Details of the rubric template are provided in Appendix A.
annotations.summary: The strict rubric design is underspecified; clarify how checklist items are constructed and sourced to enable faithful reproduction.

annotations.text: Baselines. We compare against: (1) View1-only: standard judge with CoT included; (2) View2- only: judge with CoT removed; (3) Strict-always: evidence-anchored rubric applied to all trajectories; (4) Random Escalation: escalates a random 10% of trajectories to strict rubric.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) The experimental setup is clearly specified: AgentRewardBench with 1,106 trajectories, Progress Fabrication attack on 811 failures, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct as judge, and four baselines.

(Diagnosis) One critical issue: the baselines include "Random Escalation" at a fixed 10% rate, but the paper's method escalates 10.4% of trajectories (Table 2). While this is close, the comparison should be explicitly rate-matched to ensure fairness. The Matched-Cost Control in Table 2 attempts to address this, but the main table comparison should also note that the escalation rates are similar.

(Risk) Without explicit rate-matching justification, reviewers could argue that the Random Escalation baseline is unfairly disadvantaged if it misses critical attacked trajectories that the targeted escalation catches.

(Mentor Revised Version) Baselines. We compare against: (1) View1-only: standard judge with CoT included; (2) View2-only: judge with CoT removed; (3) Strict-always: evidence-anchored rubric applied to all trajectories; (4) Random Escalation: escalates a random 10% of trajectories to strict rubric, matching the approximate escalation rate of our method (10.4%) to ensure fair comparison under similar compute budgets.
annotations.summary: Random Escalation baseline should explicitly state rate-matching with the proposed method's 10.4% escalation rate for fair comparison.

annotations.text: Figure 2 validates our mechanistic hypothesis that CoT manipulation causes disproportionate disagreement between views. The disagreement rate on attacked failures (16.4%) is 2.15× higher than on unmodified failures (7.6%), confirming that when CoT is manipulated, View1 predictions shift while View2 remains stable. This enrichment demonstrates that view disagreement is an informative signal for detecting manipulation attempts.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) Section 4.3 reports that disagreement on attacked failures (16.4%) is 2.15× higher than on unmodified failures (7.6%), validating the mechanistic hypothesis. This is a key result supporting the core claim.

(Diagnosis) The phrase "View2 remains stable" is repeated here from the hypothesis statement, but the 7.6% disagreement rate on unmodified failures indicates that View2 is not perfectly stable—some disagreement occurs even without manipulation. A more precise interpretation would be that manipulation increases disagreement beyond the baseline disagreement rate, rather than that View2 is fully stable.

(Risk) Overstating View2 stability could mislead readers about the specificity of the disagreement signal. The 7.6% baseline disagreement means that ~8% of unmanipulated failures trigger unnecessary escalation, which is a non-trivial cost.

(Mentor Revised Version) Figure 2 validates our mechanistic hypothesis that CoT manipulation causes disproportionate disagreement between views. The disagreement rate on attacked failures (16.4%) is 2.15× higher than on unmodified failures (7.6%), confirming that when CoT is manipulated, View1 predictions shift more than View2 predictions. This enrichment demonstrates that view disagreement is an informative signal for detecting manipulation attempts. We note that the baseline disagreement rate of 7.6% on unmodified failures reflects inherent judgment variability from CoT removal; our method leverages the asymmetric increase in disagreement rather than assuming perfect View2 stability.
annotations.summary: Section 4.3 repeats the "View2 remains stable" claim; clarify that the 7.6% baseline disagreement shows View2 is not perfectly stable, and the signal is asymmetric rather than absolute.

annotations.text: We presented view-disagreement escalation, a training-free framework for improving the robustness of LLM-based trajectory judges against CoT manipulation attacks. By comparing judgments from counterfactual input views (with and without CoT) and selectively escalating disagreeing cases to evidence-anchored evaluation, our method achieves a 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity while maintaining competitive accuracy and achieving the best recall among all evaluated methods. The 2.15× disagreement enrichment under attack validates the mechanistic hypothesis underlying our approach. A limitation is the higher inference cost (2.1× calls per trajectory); future work could explore cost-efficient variants or extend evaluation to other attack types.
annotations.comment:
(Audit) The Conclusion summarizes the key results accurately: 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity, competitive accuracy, best recall, and 2.15× disagreement enrichment. It also identifies a practical limitation (2.1× inference cost).

(Diagnosis) The conclusion is concise and does not introduce new unsupported claims, which is good. However, the limitation discussion is brief. The 2.1× cost is noted, but the conclusion does not mention other important limitations, such as: (a) the method only addresses Progress Fabrication attacks and has not been tested against style-based manipulations or other attack types; (b) the approach is evaluated on a single judge model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) and its generalization to other models is unknown.

(Risk) A single-sentence limitation statement underplays the scope constraints of the work. Reviewers may perceive this as hiding limitations rather than honestly bounding them.

(Mentor Revised Version) We presented view-disagreement escalation, a training-free framework for improving the robustness of LLM-based trajectory judges against CoT manipulation attacks. By comparing judgments from counterfactual input views (with and without CoT) and selectively escalating disagreeing cases to evidence-anchored evaluation, our method achieves a 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity while maintaining competitive accuracy and achieving the best recall among all evaluated methods. The 2.15× disagreement enrichment under attack validates the mechanistic hypothesis underlying our approach. Limitations include the higher inference cost (2.1× calls per trajectory), evaluation on a single attack type (Progress Fabrication), and use of a single judge model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct). Future work could explore cost-efficient variants, evaluation against additional attack strategies (e.g., style-based manipulations), and generalization across judge models and task domains.
annotations.summary: Conclusion limitation statement is too brief; expand to cover single attack type, single judge model, and cost constraints for honest scope bounding.
